title: Question 8

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: For the free electrons moving in the slice:
parts.text: state the direction of the force on an electron due to movement of the electron in the magnetic field
hints: Hint 1: Picture the two directions you know - the electron velocity into the slice and the magnetic field B across the slice - and remember you need a direction perpendicular to both for the force.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sort out velocity and field directions**
Think of the electrons entering face PQKJ and moving straight into the slice, while the field $B$ points horizontally across the slice. The magnetic force must be at right angles to both.

Step 2: **Apply Fleming's left-hand rule carefully**
For negative electrons, the conventional current is opposite to the electron motion. Using $F = Bqv$ with the left hand gives a force directed vertically downwards, toward the bottom of the slice.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: identify the faces, using the letters on Fig. 8.1, between which a potential difference is developed.
hints: Hint 1: If the magnetic force pushes all the free electrons toward one side, which pair of opposite faces will gain excess electrons and which will be left positive?
parts.proper_answer: Face PQRS and face JKLM, i.e. the top and bottom faces.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Follow where the electrons pile up**
The downward magnetic force in (a)(i) drives electrons to the bottom face. That face becomes negative while the opposite top face is left positive.

Step 2: **Name the faces**
From Fig. 8.1 the top face is PQRS and the bottom face is JKLM. The Hall p.d. therefore develops between face PQRS and face JKLM.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Explain why the potential difference in (a)(ii) reaches a maximum value.

markscheme_points.text: (as charge separates) an electric field is created (between opposite faces)
(maximum value is reached when) electric force (on electron) is equal and opposite to magnetic force (on electron)

hints: Hint 1: Think about the separation of charge: as electrons are deflected to one face, an electric field develops across the slice.
Hint 2: In the steady state, the electric force on an electron balances the magnetic force, preventing further charge accumulation.
parts.proper_answer: Separated charge sets up a transverse electric field E across the slice. This exerts an electric force $eE$ on electrons opposite to the magnetic force $Bev$. When $eE = Bev$ no further deflection occurs, so the Hall p.d. $V_H = Ed$ reaches a steady maximum.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Charge separation creates an electric field**
As electrons accumulate on one face, that face becomes negative and the opposite face positive. This is like a parallel-plate capacitor, so a transverse electric field $E$ builds up across the slice.

Step 2: **A new opposing force appears**
Any further electron moving through now feels an electric force: $$F_E = eE$$ This acts upwards, opposite to the downward magnetic force: $$F_B = Bev$$

Step 3: **Equilibrium gives maximum p.d.**
As more charge piles up, $E$ and $F_E$ grow. Very quickly: $$eE = Bev$$ The net transverse force becomes zero, electrons stop being deflected, and the p.d. $V_H$ across the faces stops increasing at its maximum value.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The number of free electrons per unit volume in the slice of material is $1.3 \times 10^{29}\text{m}^{-3}$.
The thickness PQ of the slice is $0.10\text{mm}$.
The magnetic flux density $B$ is $4.6 \times 10^{-3}\text{T}$.

Calculate the potential difference across the slice for a current of $6.3 \times 10^{-4}\text{A}$.
hints: Hint 1: Use the Hall voltage formula $V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq}$, identifying which dimension represents the thickness $t$ parallel to the magnetic field.
Hint 2: Substitute $B$, $I$, $n$, elementary charge $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, and $t$ in metres to calculate the Hall voltage.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write the Hall equation**
At equilibrium $V_H$ is given by: $$V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq}$$ where $t$ is the thickness PQ $= 0.10 \text{ mm}$, $n = 1.3 \times 10^{29} \text{ m}^{-3}$, $B = 4.6 \times 10^{-3} \text{ T}$, $I = 6.3 \times 10^{-4} \text{ A}$ and $q = e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

Step 2: **Convert thickness to SI**
$$t = 0.10 \text{ mm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$$

Step 3: **Substitute and calculate**
$$V_H = \frac{(4.6 \times 10^{-3})(6.3 \times 10^{-4})}{(1.3 \times 10^{29})(1.0 \times 10^{-4})(1.60 \times 10^{-19})}$$ $$V_H = \frac{2.90 \times 10^{-6}}{2.08 \times 10^{6}} \approx 1.4 \times 10^{-12} \text{ V}$$ This is the steady transverse p.d. across the slice.

parts.label: (d)
parts.part_stem: The slice in (c) is a metal.
parts.text: By reference to your answer in (c), suggest why Hall probes are usually made using semiconductors rather than metals.

markscheme_points.text: semiconductors have a (much) smaller value for n
V_H for semiconductors is (much) larger so more easily measured

hints: Hint 1: Note that the Hall voltage in a metal is of the order of $10^{-12}\text{ V}$, which is extremely difficult to measure.
Hint 2: Semiconductors have a much lower charge carrier density $n$, and since $V_H \propto \frac{1}{n}$, the resulting Hall voltage is much larger and easier to measure.
parts.proper_answer: Metals have very large $n$, giving $V_H \approx 10^{-12} \text{ V}$ which is too small to measure. Semiconductors have much smaller $n$, so $V_H = BI/ntq$ is much larger and easily measurable, making a more sensitive Hall probe.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Judge the metal result**
In (c) $V_H \approx 1.4 \times 10^{-12} \text{ V}$. That is picovolt level, far too tiny to measure reliably with ordinary voltmeters and easily lost in noise.

Step 2: **Compare carrier densities**
A metal has a huge free-electron density $n \sim 10^{29} \text{ m}^{-3}$. A semiconductor has a much smaller $n$, by many orders of magnitude, because only few charge carriers are available.

Step 3: **Link to Hall sensitivity**
Since: $$V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq} \propto \frac{1}{n}$$ a smaller $n$ gives a much larger $V_H$ for the same $B$, $I$ and $t$. Semiconductors therefore give a large, measurable Hall voltage and make practical, sensitive Hall probes.
